'''Greg N. Stephanopoulos''' (born {{circa}} 1950) is an American chemical engineer and the Willard Henry Dow Professor in the department of chemical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He has worked at [[MIT]], [[Caltech]], and the [[University of Minnesota]] in the areas of [[biotechnology]], [[bioinformatics]], and [[metabolic engineering]]<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://cheme.mit.edu/profile/gregory-stephanopoulos/|title=MIT - Greg Stephanopoulos|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref> especially in the areas of bioprocessing for biochemical and biofuel production. Stephanopoulos is the author of over 400 scientific publications with more than 35,000 citations (h index = 97) as of April 2018.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=S-DzIpYAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra|title=Google Scholar - Greg Stephanopoulos|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>  In addition, Greg has supervised more than 70 graduate students and 50 post-docs whose research has led to more than 50 patents.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://cme.uchicago.edu/sites/cme.uchicago.edu/files/Stephanopoulos%20CV%20and%20flyer%202017-03-06.pdf|title=2017 CV - Greg Stephanopoulos|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref> He was elected a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (2005), a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2003), and received the [[ENI award|ENI Prize on Renewable Energy]] 2011.

==Early life and education ==
He completed his Ph.D. in chemical engineering at the [[University of Minnesota]] in 1975, with advisors [[Arnold Fredrickson]] and [[Rutherford Aris]] on the topic of modeling of [[population dynamics]]. His thesis was published in 1978 with the title, "Mathematical Modelling of the Dynamics of Interacting Microbial Populations.  Extinction Probabilities in a Stochastic Competition and Predation".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Thesis - Greg. N. Stephanopoulos|id = {{ProQuest|302880179}}}}</ref>

== Career ==
Stephanopoulos began his career as an assistant professor of chemical engineering at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1978. He was promoted to associate professor in 1978. In 1985, he was hired by the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as professor of chemical engineering. During his time at MIT, he has held the following positions:  associate director, Biotechnology Center (1990-1997), professor of the MIT-Harvard Division of Health Science and Technology - HST (2000–Present), Bayer Professor of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology (2000 - 2005), and the W. H. Dow Professor of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology (2006–Present). From 2006 to 2007, he was a visiting professor at the Institute for Chemical and Bioengineering in [[Zürich]], Switzerland.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://cme.uchicago.edu/sites/cme.uchicago.edu/files/Stephanopoulos%20CV%20and%20flyer%202017-03-06.pdf|title=Abstract - Greg Stephanopoulos|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>

As noted in the citation for his ENI Prize, Stephanopoulos's research has addressed the advancement of multiple aspects bioengineering:

{{quote
|text=  He is mostly renowned for his studies on the global transcription machinery engineering technology, concerning the reprogramming of the gene transcription of particular bacteria, in order to modify their microbial cells, increasing their efficiency in transformation of raw material in hydrocarbons.  Until now, the best result concerns the increase in tolerance of microbial cultivations to the toxicity of several products, and the consequent, relevant increase of productiveness in biofuels.
|author=ENI Award Citation, 2011<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.eni.com/docs/en_IT/enipedia/business-model/eni-awards/2011/gregory_stephanopoulos.pdf|title=ENI Award Citation - Greg Stephanopoulos|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
}}

== Honors ==

In 2003, Stephanopoulos was elected a member of the American National Academy of Engineering (NAE). His NAE election citation noted:<ref>{{cite web|title=Dr. Gregory Stephanopoulos|url=https://www.nae.edu/30436/Dr-Gregory-Stephanopoulos|website=National Academy of Engineering|access-date=13 April 2026
}}</ref>
{{quote
|text=For pioneering contributions in defining and advancing metabolic engineering and for leadership in incorporating biology into chemical engineering research and education.
|author=Election Citation, National Academy of Engineering, 2003
}}

Other awards and honors include: 
*AIChE R.H. Wilhelm Award in Chemical Reaction Engineering (2001)<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/awards/r-h-wilhelm-award-chemical-reaction-engineering|title=AIChE Wilhelm Award|date=28 March 2012 |accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
*Elected to the National Academy of Engineering (2002)<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nae.edu/30436.aspx|title=NAE Gregory Stephanopoulos|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
*Elected Fellow of AAAS (2005)<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellow/stephanopoulos-gregory|title=AAAS Gregory Stephanopoulos|journal=AAAS - the World's Largest General Scientific Society |date=17 May 2017 |accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
*AIChE Founders Award (2007)<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/awards/founders-award-outstanding-contributions-field-chemical-engineering|title=AIChE Founders Award|date=28 March 2012 |accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
*Amgen Biochemical Engineering Award (2009)<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2009-06/eci-gsw062909.php|title=Greg Stephanopoulos: Amgen Biochemical Engineering Award|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
* ENI Prize in Renewable and Non-Conventional Energy (2011)<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.eni.com/enipedia/en_IT/business-model/awards-recognition/eni-award-2011-edition.page|title=ENI Prize 2011|accessdate=2 March 2018}}</ref>
*Elected Fellow, American Academy of Microbiology (2013)
*Elected President of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers (2015)
